name: Epitiostanol

lead: Epitiostanol is a dihydrotestosterone-derived steroid that blocks the estrogen receptor while weakly activating the androgen receptor. It has been used in Japan since 1977 as an anticancer drug for breast cancer.
It shows up in muscle-related lists because it is classed as an anabolic-androgenic steroid. No published trial has tested it for muscle gain or appearance.

paras: It binds the estrogen receptor as an antagonist and the androgen receptor as an agonist. In premenopausal women it also suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, lowering estrogen. Orally it is broken down extensively in the gut wall and liver, so it has been given by injection; mepitiostane is an oral prodrug.

Little safety information is published in the sources available. A related prodrug, mepitiostane, has a high rate of virilizing effects in women. It is a prescription drug in Japan, and the related compound methylepitiostanol has appeared as a designer steroid.

lead: Epitiostanol (brand name Thiodrol) is a synthetic steroid of the dihydrotestosterone group that acts as an antiestrogen and as a comparatively weak anabolic-androgenic steroid. It has been used in Japan as an antineoplastic drug for breast cancer since 1977. [1]

Its interest to physique communities stems from its classification as an anabolic steroid. No published human study has examined it for muscle gain or other appearance outcomes. Published human work concerns hormone effects in women and breast cancer treatment. [2][3]

paras: Wikipedia reports that epitiostanol has been used in Japan to treat breast cancer since 1977 and cites studies from 1973 and 1975 on its use for gynecomastia. [1] A 1988 Japanese case report described advanced breast cancer treated with tamoxifen combined with epitiostanol. [4]

Epitiostanol is an androgen receptor agonist and an estrogen receptor antagonist. Wikipedia describes it as potent as an antiestrogen and weak as an anabolic steroid, with about eleven times the anabolic activity of methyltestosterone and roughly equal androgenic activity. In premenopausal women it also acts as an antigonadotropin, suppressing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. [1] A 1975 Japanese study examined its effects on this axis in humans. [3]

In rats given epitiostanol orally, radioactivity was absorbed but no unchanged drug was found in plasma, because of extensive first-pass metabolism in the intestinal mucosa and liver. [5] This is why the drug is injected and why the oral prodrug mepitiostane was developed. [1][6]

Epitiostanol is 2α,3α-epithio-5α-androstan-17β-ol, with the formula C19H30OS. Derivatives include mepitiostane and methylepitiostanol, an orally active 17α-methyl variant that has appeared as a designer steroid. [1]

A zebrafish chemical screen reported in 2016 identified epitiostanol, progesterone and mifepristone as small molecules that lowered ferroportin protein levels, linked to progesterone receptor membrane component-1 and hepcidin regulation. This was laboratory work on iron homeostasis, not a study of appearance. [7] Animal studies in mouse and rat mammary tumor models have also examined mepitiostane and estrogen depletion. [8]
No studies found for muscle or appearance outcomes. Published human reports concern breast cancer and effects on pituitary-gonadal hormones. [3][4]
